title: Yet they confess the beginning of justification is from God alone, man merely passive (Angles)
source_text: XIV. Quanquam vero Scholae Romanae Doctores cum Concilio Tridentino statuant liberum hominis arbitrium cooperari Deo vocanti atque excitanti, & humanam voluntatem non solum active, sed libere se habere, respectu primorum actuum quibus ad Deum convertimur; ita ut allicienti & trahenti gratiae non solum consentire, sed & ab ea dissentire possit: fatentur tamen initium justificationis & conversionis nostrae a solo Deo esse, non a libero nostro arbitrio, & eo respectu hominem mere passive se habere. Id videre est apud Josephum Angles Episcopum Bosanensem, cujus haec est Conclusio, Initium nostrae justificationis non est a libero arbitrio nostro; sed est solum ab ipso Deo, nobis mere passive nos habentibus. Quod postea multis scripturae locis probat. Ut illo, Non vos me elegistis. Item, Sine me nihil potestis facere. Et, Nemo potest venire ad me, nisi Pater meus traxerit eum. In floribus quaestionum Theologicarum, Tractatu de Libero Arbitrio, quaestione unica. Articulo 3. Difficultate 7. Conclusione 1.
pass_a_gloss: XIV. But although the Doctors of the Roman School with the Council of Trent establish that the free choice of man cooperates with God calling and arousing, and that the human will behaves not only actively, but freely, in respect of the first acts by which we are converted to God; so that it can not only consent to grace alluring and drawing, but also dissent from it: yet they confess that the beginning of our justification and conversion is from God alone, not from our free choice, and that in that respect man behaves merely passively. This may be seen in Joseph Angles Bishop of Bosa, whose Conclusion this is, The beginning of our justification is not from our free choice; but is only from God himself, we behaving merely passively. Which afterwards he proves by many places of scripture. As by that, You have not chosen me. Again, Without me you can do nothing. And, No one can come to me, unless my Father draw him. In the Flowers of Theological Questions, Treatise on Free Choice, single question. Article 3. Difficulty 7. Conclusion 1.
pass_b_english: The doctors of the Roman School, with the Council of Trent, hold that man's free choice cooperates with God as he calls and rouses it, and that the human will acts not only actively but freely in the first acts by which we turn to God, so that it can not only consent to grace that attracts and draws it but also dissent from it.

All the same, they concede that our justification and conversion start from God alone and not from our free choice, and that in this respect man is merely passive. This can be seen in Joseph Angles, Bishop of Bosa, whose conclusion reads: 'The beginning of our justification lies not in our free choice. It lies solely in God himself, while we are merely passive.'

He goes on to support it with a number of scriptural texts: 'You did not choose me'; 'Apart from me you can do nothing'; 'No one can come to me unless my Father draws him.' (Flores theologicarum quaestionum, on free choice, the single question, article 3, difficulty 7, conclusion 1.)

lemmas.latin: initium justificationis & conversionis nostrae a solo Deo esse
lemmas.gloss: the beginning of our justification and conversion is from God alone

choices.why: The will receiving God's action without acting; kept as the scholastic adverb.
